title: Kanesh and the Assyrian Colonies
subtitle: 2,000–1,650 BC · Merchants from Assur, the Princes of the Plateau and the First Archives of Anatolia

categories.label: Power
categories.subtitle: The princes of Kanesh and Burushattum, the rulers of Assur behind the colony system, and the Kussaran kings who ended it

entries.label: The princes of Kanesh — Inar and Warshama
entries.hint: Kanesh was the seat of a local ruler, styled 'prince' in the Assyrian texts, with a palace on the high mound and the colony of Assyrian merchants (the karum) in the lower town below. Inar and Warshama are named as its rulers in the merchants' records, and the palace of Warshama burned with the rest of Level II in about 1835 BC. The prince, not Assur, was the sovereign of the city.
entries.note: Kültepe tablets (Kt a/k, Kt n/k series) published by Tahsin Özgüç and later by Cécile Michel and Klaas Veenhof; Mogens Larsen, The Old Assyrian City-State and Its Colonies (1976).

entries.label: A land of rival princes
entries.hint: The Assyrian archives name dozens of small kingdoms on the plateau — Kanesh, Hahhum, Wahsusana, Durhumit, Burushattum, Hattum, Zalpa and others — each with its prince and often a queen, who made treaties with Assur and fought one another. The plateau had no single state; its map was a patchwork of walled towns and their dependent villages.
entries.note: Gojko Barjamovic, A Historical Geography of Ancient Anatolia in the Assyrian Colony Period (Copenhagen, 2011); Kültepe archives.

entries.label: Burushattum and the Sarıkaya palace
entries.hint: At Acemhöyük, probably ancient Burushattum, a palace called Sarıkaya was built around 1790 BC on timbers whose felling dates fit the late eighteenth century. It held ivory furniture, wall paintings and a store of clay sealings, among them impressions of the seals of foreign kings. The prince of Burushattum was a figure of international standing at a time when the colonies were already waning.
entries.note: Nimet Özgüç, Acemhöyük excavation reports (1960s–80s); dendrochronology on the Sarıkaya palace timbers (2016 study).

entries.label: Erishum I and the City of Assur
entries.hint: Erishum I ruled Assur, a city-state on the Tigris, whose merchants dominated the trade with Anatolia. The Level II archives at Kanesh begin in his time, and his own inscriptions in Assur mention building work for the god Assur. The city's real government was a council of leading merchants with the ruler as its executive.
entries.note: Erishum I inscriptions; Klaas Veenhof and Jesper Eidem, Mesopotamia: The Old Assyrian Period (2008).

entries.label: Shamshi-Adad I and the end of Assur's independence
entries.hint: In about 1808 BC Shamshi-Adad, an Amorite warlord from Ekallatum, took Assur and made it part of a territorial kingdom of northern Mesopotamia. He let the long-distance trade go on but under his control. Assyrian merchants lived on in Anatolia, but now as subjects of an empire whose centre was at Shubat-Enlil.
entries.note: Metropolitan Museum of Art, 'The Old Assyrian Period (ca. 2000–1600 B.C.)'; Veenhof and Eidem 2008; Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen, Ups and Downs at Kanesh (2012).

entries.label: Pithana and Anitta of Kussara
entries.hint: Kussara, a town not yet found, produced two kings whose deeds are told in the Anitta text. Pithana took Nesa (Kanesh) by night without harming its people, and his son Anitta subdued the rivals of the plateau, destroyed Hattusa, took the title of great king and made Nesa his seat. The dates are uncertain, between about 1750 and 1700 BC on different chronologies.
entries.note: Anitta text (KBo 3.22; CTH 1.A), edited by Erich Neu, StBoT 18 (1974); Trevor Bryce, The Kingdom of the Hittites (1998).

categories.label: Conflict
categories.subtitle: The burning of Level II, Shamshi-Adad's conquest of Assur and the march of Pithana and Anitta

entries.label: The burning of the Level II karum
entries.hint: Level II came to an end in a great fire that destroyed the Assyrian quarter and the palace on the mound alike, leaving the merchants' archives sealed under collapsed roofs and so preserving them. Most specialists think it was an act of war, perhaps by a rival prince. The trade resumed after an interval, and Kanesh was rebuilt as Level Ib.
entries.note: Tahsin Özgüç, Kültepe-Kaniš (1959) and later reports; Veenhof and Eidem 2008; Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen 2012.

entries.label: Shamshi-Adad takes Assur
entries.hint: Shamshi-Adad's conquest of Assur put an end to the city-state that had run the colony system. His court at Shubat-Enlil and the archives of Mari record the new order, in which his son Ishme-Dagan ruled the Tigris lands from Ekallatum. Anatolian trade continued, but the archives from Kanesh thin out sharply in the generations that followed.
entries.note: Archives of Mari; Metropolitan Museum essay on the Old Assyrian period; Veenhof and Eidem 2008.

entries.label: Pithana takes Nesa
entries.hint: The Anitta text states that Pithana, king of Kussara, took Nesa at night by force and 'did no evil to anyone in Nesa; he treated them like his mothers and fathers'. This is the earliest account in the Hittite language of a king's military deeds, and it ties the Kussaran line to the city whose name gave the Hittite language its alternative name, Nesite.
entries.note: Anitta text (KBo 3.22), StBoT 18 (1974).

entries.label: Anitta destroys Hattusa
entries.hint: Anitta defeated Huzziya of Zalpa and Piyusti of Hatti, took Hattusa and, as the text says, destroyed it and cursed it — 'whoever becomes king after me and resettles Hattusa, let the Storm God of Heaven strike him'. A later king would defy the curse and take the name Hattusili, 'man of Hattusa'.
entries.note: Anitta text (KBo 3.22), StBoT 18 (1974).

entries.label: The last fire at Kanesh
entries.hint: Level Ib too ended in fire, around 1700 BC on the most-used chronology though the date is debated. Some scholars link it to the fall of Assur's trade network, others to a campaign by a local king. The colony's records, much thinner than those of Level II, break off. Kanesh was occupied thereafter but never again as an Assyrian trading post.
entries.note: Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen, Ups and Downs at Kanesh (2012); Veenhof and Eidem 2008.

categories.label: Order
categories.subtitle: Treaties with the princes, the self-governing karum and the year-eponym that dated every contract

entries.label: The self-governing karum
entries.hint: In each colony the Assyrian merchants formed a karum, with its own assembly, its own judges and its own seal and archive, which issued judgments, collected levies and corresponded with the City Hall of Assur. Disputes between merchants were tried by the karum in Assyrian law, not by the Anatolian prince.
entries.note: Larsen 1976; Veenhof 1972; the Kültepe judicial texts.

entries.label: The year-eponym and the eponym list
entries.hint: Assyrian contracts were dated by the limum, an official chosen by lot each year whose name gave the year its label. The lists of eponyms found at Kültepe (the KEL lists) run to well over a century and are the backbone of Old Assyrian chronology, and, through it, of the Bronze Age timeline of the whole Near East.
entries.note: Kültepe Eponym Lists (KEL A–G); Veenhof, 'The Old Assyrian List of Year Eponyms' (2003); Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen 2012.

entries.label: Loans, witnesses and the written contract
entries.hint: Debts, partnerships and sales were recorded in sealed tablets before witnesses, with interest, a repayment date and penalties written out. A commercial law had developed in which the written, sealed contract was the proof and the karum's judges the enforcers.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972 and 2020; Cécile Michel, Correspondance des marchands de Kaniš (2001).

entries.label: The treaties between Assur and the princes
entries.hint: The Assyrian merchants worked in Anatolia under sworn agreements between the city of Assur, the karum and each local prince. These regulated import duties, the prince's right to buy goods first, safe passage and the handling of crimes and debts. The merchants paid taxes to the rulers in return for protection, and the karum was held responsible for their conduct.
entries.note: Klaas Veenhof, Aspects of Old Assyrian Trade and Its Terminology (1972); Veenhof, Law and Trade in Ancient Mesopotamia and Anatolia (2020).

categories.label: Belief
categories.subtitle: Oaths on the dagger of Assur, the weather god on Anatolian seals and the dead beneath the merchants' floors

entries.label: The dagger of Assur
entries.hint: The merchants swore their most solemn oaths on the dagger of the god Assur, the patron of their city, and kept a fund for his temple. Their letters invoke Assur, Ishtar and the Storm god. The god of a small city on the Tigris travelled by donkey 1,000 kilometres to the plateau with those who believed in him.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972; Michel, Correspondance des marchands de Kaniš (2001).

entries.label: The dead beneath the merchants' floors
entries.hint: The people of Kanesh buried their dead beneath the floors of the houses, in pits or in jars, with pottery, jewellery and weapons. The burial customs of the karum are largely Anatolian, so the graves themselves rarely reveal whether a person was Assyrian or local; the archives, not the cemetery, show who lived there.
entries.note: Tahsin Özgüç, Kültepe-Kaniš (1959) and Kültepe and Its Vicinity (1986).

entries.label: The weather god and the goddess on Anatolian seals
entries.hint: Seals in the local style show a storm god standing on a bull, a nude goddess, a goddess holding a vessel, and a god with a sceptre, with mixed local and Syrian-Mesopotamian features. The weather god — later Tarhunna among the Luwians and Teshub among the Hurrians — was the plateau's chief deity.
entries.note: Nimet Özgüç, Seals and Seal Impressions of Level Ib from Karum Kanish (Ankara, 1968) and The Anatolian Group of Cylinder Seal Impressions from Kültepe (1965).

categories.label: Expression
categories.subtitle: Anatolian and Assyrian seals, painted Cappadocian ware, the palaces of Kanesh and Acemhöyük

entries.label: Anatolian and Assyrian seal styles
entries.hint: Some thousands of impressions on the clay envelopes of the tablets show several seal styles side by side: Old Assyrian, Old Babylonian, Syrian and a distinctive local Anatolian one with processions, banquets, animals and mythical scenes. Together they form the biggest corpus of Bronze Age seal impressions with a firm date.
entries.note: Nimet Özgüç 1965 and 1968; Beatrice Teissier, Sealing and Seals on Texts from Kültepe Kārum Level 2 (1994).

entries.label: Cappadocian painted ware and animal vessels
entries.hint: Local potters made brightly painted wares with geometric designs in brown on a cream slip, and spouted jugs, 'teapots', and vessels in the shapes of birds and bulls. Cappadocian painted ware is among the best known products of the plateau in the Middle Bronze Age.
entries.note: Tahsin Özgüç, Kültepe-Kaniš (1959); Kültepe excavation reports (Özgüç and Fikri Kulakoğlu).

entries.label: The palaces of Kanesh and Acemhöyük
entries.hint: The palace of the prince of Kanesh stood on the upper mound, and the Sarıkaya palace at Acemhöyük had large courtyards, many storerooms and rooms with painted plaster. The merchants' houses of the lower town had stone foundations and mudbrick walls around courtyards, with rooms set aside for archives.
entries.note: Özgüç, Kültepe and Its Vicinity (1986); Özgüç, Acemhöyük reports.

entries.label: A harp on a seal from Konya-Karahöyük
entries.hint: A cylinder seal impression from Konya-Karahöyük shows a goddess, read as Ishtar, playing a harp before a god, read as Ea. Anatolian art of this age includes harps and lyres on cylinder seals, and no instrument survives, but the sealing shows that performance accompanied cult and court scenes.
entries.note: Sedat Alp, Konya civarında Karahöyük kazısında bulunan silindir ve damga mühürleri (1968); studies of Anatolian music iconography.

categories.label: Thought
categories.subtitle: The letters of the merchants, the first Indo-European names and the Anitta text

entries.label: The merchants' letters
entries.hint: Over twenty thousand tablets from Kanesh include thousands of letters between merchants, their partners at Assur and their wives and families, in a direct, practical, often irritated voice. They are the earliest large archive of private correspondence in the world and the first writing of any kind in Anatolia.
entries.note: Kültepe tablets; Cécile Michel, Correspondance des marchands de Kaniš (2001); Michel, Women of Aššur and Kaneš (SBL, 2020).

entries.label: The first Indo-European names
entries.hint: The Assyrian texts record Anatolian princes and townspeople with names that are Hattic, Hurrian and, many of them, of the Indo-European Anatolian family — Anitta, Pithana and Warshama among them — and a few words of Hittite, Luwian and Palaic. They give the first writing of the languages later used in the Hittite state.
entries.note: Kültepe tablets; Hoffner and Melchert 2008; Kloekhorst's studies on Old Anatolian names.

entries.label: The Anitta text
entries.hint: The Anitta text survives in copies from the Hittite archive and tells the deeds of Pithana and Anitta of Kussara in the Hittite language. It is the oldest narrative composition in an Indo-European language, and a written memory of the plateau's rulers across the Karum age. Its original date is placed in the seventeenth century BC or later, and some scholars suggest an Akkadian original.
entries.note: Anitta text (KBo 3.22, CTH 1.A), StBoT 18 (Neu, 1974); Alfonso Archi on the Akkadian original; Kloekhorst and de Waal (2019).

categories.label: Economy
categories.subtitle: Tin and cloth for silver and gold, the wool of Assur, loans at interest and Anatolian copper

entries.label: Tin and cloth for silver and gold
entries.hint: Assyrian merchants sold tin from the east and textiles from Babylonia and their own households in Anatolia, and sent silver and gold back to Assur. One estimate puts the trade of the best-attested years (1895–1865 BC) at some 1,500 donkey-loads a year, several tons of tin and thousands of textiles. Profit margins were high and the risks were theft, tolls and the loss of animals on the roads.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972 and 2020; Metropolitan Museum essay on the Old Assyrian period; Larsen 1976.

entries.label: The household cloth of Assur
entries.hint: Women in Assur wove the textiles that went to Anatolia, in household workshops, from wool supplied by the merchant families and sold at a profit. The letters show the wives specifying quality, price and colour, and complaining when the cloth did not sell.
entries.note: Cécile Michel, Women of Aššur and Kaneš (SBL, 2020); Michel, Correspondance des marchands de Kaniš (2001).

entries.label: Silver, loans and interest
entries.hint: Silver, weighed out by standard weights, was the money of the colonies — there was no coinage — and loans on silver were often made at interest of about 30 per cent a year. Merchants made partnerships and invested capital with others through written contracts, creating a credit economy.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972 and 2020; Larsen 1976.

entries.label: Anatolian copper
entries.hint: Alongside the tin and textiles, Assyrian merchants bought and re-sold copper within Anatolia, using local metal for exchange between the plateau's towns. The metal trade tied the colonies to the local economy and made them a part of it, not just visitors.
entries.note: Metropolitan Museum essay on the Old Assyrian period; Veenhof 1972.

categories.label: Technology
categories.subtitle: The sealed clay envelope, a business script and iron as a precious metal

entries.label: The sealed envelope and the business script
entries.hint: The merchants wrote in a streamlined cuneiform syllabary of a few hundred signs that could be learned quickly, on small clay tablets, enclosed in clay envelopes that carried the seals of the witnesses. A clay envelope was both a legal safeguard and an archive of seals.
entries.note: Kültepe tablets; Veenhof 1972; Michel 2001.

entries.label: Iron as a precious metal
entries.hint: The texts mention a metal called amutum, translated as meteoritic or early iron, valued at many times the price of silver. It was worked in small quantities as an object of prestige: in the Anitta text a king of Purushanda is said to have brought an iron throne and an iron sceptre to Anitta. Iron was rare luxury, and the Iron Age was still a thousand years off.
entries.note: Kültepe tablets (Veenhof 1972 on amutum); Anitta text (KBo 3.22).

entries.label: The caravan road and its stations
entries.hint: The road from Assur to Kanesh crossed some 1,000 kilometres of steppe, river and mountain, with way-stations, guides and tolls at each principality. A caravan took weeks, and travel itineraries and costs were written down in detail by the merchants.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972; Barjamovic 2011 on itineraries.

categories.label: Exchange
categories.subtitle: The donkey road from Assur, the tin route from the east and the foreign seals of Acemhöyük

entries.label: The donkey road from Assur to Kanesh
entries.hint: Caravans of donkeys carried tin and cloth from Assur to some forty Anatolian settlements, of which Kanesh was the main karum and the others smaller trading posts (wabartum). The network was the first documented long-distance trading diaspora in history.
entries.note: Metropolitan Museum essay on the Old Assyrian period; Veenhof 2020; Barjamovic 2011.

entries.label: The tin route from the east
entries.hint: Assyrian merchants bought tin from the Iranian plateau in the east — through intermediaries — and textiles from Babylonia in the south, and re-sold both in Anatolia. The source of the tin is still uncertain, with Iranian and Central Asian deposits both proposed.
entries.note: Metropolitan Museum essay on the Old Assyrian period; Veenhof 2020; Yener, The Domestication of Metals (2000).

entries.label: The foreign kings' seals at Acemhöyük
entries.hint: Impressions in the bullae room of the Sarıkaya palace carried the seals of Shamshi-Adad I, of Aplahanda of Carchemish and of Dugedu, a daughter of Yahdun-Lim of Mari. They are the physical remains of gifts and correspondence between the prince of Burushattum and the courts of Syria and Mesopotamia.
entries.note: Nimet Özgüç, Acemhöyük excavation reports (1978 campaign, bullae room of the Sarıkaya palace).

categories.label: World
categories.subtitle: A land of city-states and the end of the Karum Age

entries.label: A land of city-states
entries.hint: The plateau was divided among dozens of small states with rulers called princes. None dominated, and the Assyrian merchants worked with all of them. Their archives record a political map that would be swept away by the Hittite state a century later.
entries.note: Barjamovic 2011; Larsen 1976.

entries.label: The end of the Karum age
entries.hint: After the burning of Level Ib the Assyrian colonies faded and writing disappeared from Anatolia for generations, until the clay archives of the Hittite state. The long gap leaves historians reconstructing the rise of Kussara and Hatti from a few later texts.
entries.note: Barjamovic, Hertel and Larsen 2012; Bryce 1998.

categories.label: Lives
categories.subtitle: The letters of Taram-Kubi, an Anatolian wife and the people held in debt

entries.label: Taram-Kubi and the wives of Assur
entries.hint: Taram-Kubi wrote to her husband Innaya in Kanesh complaining of famine and a lack of money, and telling him how she ran the household and sold cloth. She is one of the many women who ran households, produced textiles, owned property and managed money while husbands were away for years.
entries.note: Cécile Michel, Women of Aššur and Kaneš: Texts from the Archives of Assyrian Merchants (SBL, 2020).

entries.label: An Anatolian wife in the Assyrian archives
entries.hint: Many Assyrian merchants took a second, local wife in Kanesh, as the marriage contracts show, and their Anatolian wives and children appear in the archives alongside the families in Assur. One of them, Kunnaniya, writes as a lonely woman left behind. The merchants' communities were bicultural from the start.
entries.note: Michel 2020; Veenhof 2020 on marriage contracts.

entries.label: Slaves and the people in pledge
entries.hint: The archives record the sale of enslaved servants, mostly women and children, and debtors or their dependants who were given over as pledges against loans. These people are visible only through the contracts that disposed of them, and their own words do not survive.
entries.note: Veenhof 1972 and 2020; Michel 2020.
